items.passage:
I gave you the fishing rod on your twelfth birthday, Errol,
and you leaned it in the corner like a broom.
Consuelo said you wanted books. I heard her
the way the river hears a pebble.
Now we stand on the stone bridge over the Hope,
you with your satchel, I with nothing in my hands,
and neither of us looks down at the water
where I used to fish at your age.
You point to a heron, stiff as a nail.
I almost tell you that my father gave me nothing,
that the rod was my whole vocabulary.
Instead I count the stones in the railing,
each one set by someone who did not explain it.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the way the river hears a pebble” most nearly suggests
options: that the speaker took in Consuelo's words without changing his course.
that the speaker found Consuelo's remark sharp and painful to accept.
that Consuelo spoke so softly the speaker could not make out her words.
that the speaker and Consuelo often argued by the river about Errol.
items.explanation: 강은 조약돌이 떨어져도 잠깐 물결이 일 뿐 흐름을 바꾸지 않는다. 화자는 아들이 책을 원한다는 Consuelo의 말을 들었지만 여전히 낚싯대를 선물했고, 그것이 자신의 유일한 '어휘'였다고 고백한다. 즉 말을 듣긴 했으나 행동은 바뀌지 않았다는 뜻이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 충격을, C는 소리 크기를 비유의 뜻으로 오해한 것이고, D는 근거가 없다.

items.passage: Piper had captained the girls' team at our school in Vigo for three seasons, and by the night of the winter dinner she ran the gymnasium like a deck: tables in rows, chairs squared, her grandmother's empanadas at the head. Lucia had arrived from Buenos Aires in October and came along that evening without being on any list; I think she slipped in behind the volunteers carrying folding chairs. She brought a tray of alfajores and set it down, hesitating, at the far corner. I watched Piper notice it. She said nothing. She lifted her grandmother's platter and slid it down the table until the two trays touched, then pulled up a chair at that end, the wrong end by her own rules, and sat. For the rest of the night the table listed toward Lucia's corner, a boat trimmed to an unexpected weight, and no one tried to set it straight.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a boat trimmed to an unexpected weight” most nearly suggests
options: that the table was overloaded with food and close to collapsing.
that the gathering had rebalanced itself around the newcomer.
that Piper had lost control of the dinner she carefully planned.
that the guests were uneasy and wished Lucia had stayed home.
items.explanation: Piper는 체육관을 배의 갑판처럼 엄격히 정돈했지만, Lucia의 쟁반을 보고 말없이 할머니의 접시를 옮겨 붙이고 자신의 규칙상 '잘못된' 끝자리에 앉는다. 배가 새 무게에 맞춰 균형을 잡는다는 비유는 모임 전체가 새로 온 사람을 중심으로 다시 자리 잡았다는 뜻이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 비유를 물리적으로 읽은 오독이다. C와 D는 기운 테이블을 실패나 불편으로 본 표면 해석으로, 아무도 바로잡지 않았다는 서술과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Three rules governed the galley of the training ship docked at Manila that summer: knives point down, nothing left on the burners, and no one cries where the cook can see. I was nineteen, newly hired to teach English to the cadets, and Anh, the cook, let me hold class at his steel tables between meals. Shira, the quietest cadet, would not answer me for weeks. So I made a plan. I asked her to translate Anh's recipes for the others, and she did, fluently, in front of everyone. The cadets applauded. Anh grinned. Shira folded the recipe card into smaller and smaller squares until it was the size of a stamp. That night I scrubbed the same pot three times. The plan had worked, I kept telling myself; the success sat in me like a meal eaten standing up.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like a meal eaten standing up” most nearly suggests
options: that the narrator was too busy teaching to sit down and eat properly.
that the narrator felt physically ill from rough conditions aboard ship.
that the narrator's achievement felt hasty and gave no real satisfaction.
that the narrator was eager to celebrate the success with the whole crew.
items.explanation: 계획은 성공해 박수가 나왔지만, Shira는 레시피 카드를 우표 크기까지 접으며 불편함을 드러낸다. 화자가 같은 냄비를 세 번 닦고 '성공했다'고 스스로를 설득하는 모습도 마음이 편치 않음을 보여 준다. 서서 급히 먹은 식사의 비유는 성공이 허겁지겁 지나가 아무런 포만감을 주지 않았다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A와 B는 비유를 글자 그대로 읽었고, D는 화자의 불편한 심정과 반대된다.

items.passage: Two cups of espresso cooled on the zinc counter of the station cafe in Bologna while Fiorella untied the ribbon around their mother's letters. Anneke's train to Rotterdam left at 4:10, and her suitcase held everything she meant to keep. They read the first letters aloud, laughing at the spelling, at the recipes copied into the margins, at a long complaint about a neighbor's goat. Fiorella did the voices. Then Anneke unfolded one dated the spring she had first gone away, years ago, and read it silently. Fiorella waited for the voice, and none came. Anneke set the page face down, squared it against the others, and picked up her ticket, turning it over as though it might list a different time. Fiorella retied the ribbon slowly, making the bow twice.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From bitter resentment of the mother to forgiving acceptance of her flaws
From playful shared reminiscence to a hushed tension about the departure
From anxious haste about the train to relief that there is time to spare
From detached curiosity about the letters to open grief expressed in tears
items.explanation: 전반부에서 두 사람은 편지를 소리 내어 읽으며 철자와 염소 이야기에 웃고, Fiorella는 목소리 연기까지 한다. Anneke가 처음 떠났던 봄의 편지를 말없이 읽는 순간부터 웃음은 사라지고, 기차표를 뒤집어 보거나 리본을 천천히 두 번 묶는 동작으로 긴장이 드러난다. 따라서 장난스러운 회상에서 이별을 앞둔 조용한 긴장으로 바뀌는 B가 정답이다. D는 눈물을 흘린다고 했지만 지문의 감정은 끝까지 겉으로 드러나지 않는다.

items.passage: Clay forgives nothing. Tamika's husband had said that to every student who walked into the studio on Seventy-First Street, and for thirty years the neighborhood had repeated it as proof of his genius. She was boxing his glazes when Ngozi arrived with the kiln parts, a lanky boy who lingered to admire the famous blue bowls on the top shelf. My uncle fired those, he said cheerfully. Your husband paid him in lunch. Tamika laughed, assuming a joke, and handed him a bowl to carry. Ngozi turned it over and showed her the mark scratched faintly into the foot, two initials that were not her husband's. She set the box of glazes down. For a while she simply moved along the shelf, bowl by bowl, turning each one over with care.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From grief-stricken mourning to cheerful celebration of the husband's work
From suspicious hostility toward Ngozi to grateful trust in his account
From affectionate pride in a legacy to a sober, searching reconsideration
From casual indifference about the bowls to an outraged public accusation
items.explanation: 도입부는 남편의 말이 동네에서 천재성의 증거로 반복되었다고 전하며 유산에 대한 자부심을 보여 준다. Tamika는 처음에 Ngozi의 말을 농담으로 여겨 웃지만, 그릇 바닥의 다른 이니셜을 본 뒤 상자를 내려놓고 그릇을 하나하나 뒤집어 본다. 이 변화는 분노가 아니라 차분히 사실을 다시 따져 보는 태도이므로 C가 정답이다. D는 공개적으로 비난한다고 했지만 그녀는 아무 말도 하지 않는다.

items.passage:
Once a week the language school in Surabaya
lent its back classroom to anyone with a map.
Thida came from the rice terraces with mud on her sandals,
Neema from the city office with a rolled survey,
and for an hour they practiced polite English,
would you, could you, may I, laughing at the verbs.
Then Neema asked her to the ministry dinner,
where the new road would be announced.
Thida closed her notebook.
She studied the whiteboard where the teacher
had written, in blue, the word boundary,
and did not erase it, and did not answer,
and thanked Neema, very correctly, for the invitation.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From formal distance to growing warmth as the two practice together
From confusion about English verbs to confident mastery of the lesson
From enthusiasm about the new road to disappointment at its delay
From easy shared amusement to guarded courtesy after the invitation
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 두 사람은 공손한 영어 표현을 연습하며 동사를 두고 함께 웃는다. 그러나 새 도로 발표 만찬 초대를 받은 뒤 Thida는 공책을 덮고 'boundary'라는 단어를 바라보며 대답 없이 '매우 정확하게' 감사만 표한다. 앞에서 연습하던 공손함이 거리를 두는 수단으로 바뀌므로 D가 정답이다. A는 변화의 방향을 거꾸로 읽은 것이고, B와 C는 지문에 근거가 없다.

items.passage: After my grandfather's funeral in Porto Alegre, I volunteered to carry the folding chairs back up to the fourth floor, mostly so I would not have to talk. I was Fausto, the grandson who had read the eulogy, and I was proud of it; people squeezed my arm on the stairs and said how well I had captured him. On the third landing Joaquim, his oldest friend, stopped me and took two of the chairs. Lovely speech, he said. Then, while adjusting his grip, he mentioned that my grandfather had never fished a day in his life; the river stories had been Joaquim's own, told so often over dominoes that they had changed owners. He said it lightly. He carried the chairs the rest of the way. I climbed behind him counting the steps, which I had never once counted before.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From self-satisfied pride to quiet, chastened reflection
From fresh grief over the death to amusement at Joaquim
From resentment of Joaquim to admiration for his kindness
From nervous dread about speaking to relief at its success
items.explanation: 초반에 Fausto는 추도사를 자랑스러워하고, 사람들의 칭찬을 그대로 받아들인다. Joaquim이 강 이야기가 사실 자신의 것이었다고 가볍게 알려 준 뒤, Fausto는 말없이 뒤따라 오르며 처음으로 계단 수를 센다. 이 행동은 자신의 실수를 조용히 되새기는 마음을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 Joaquim의 가벼운 말투만 보고 웃음으로 읽은 오독이고, C는 처음부터 원망이 있었다는 근거가 없다.

items.passage: We met in the reading room of the national library in Hanoi because neither of us could raise his voice there. Bao, my older brother, had brought the shop's ledger, and I, Dayoung, had brought nothing but the acceptance letter from the university in Seoul. For twenty minutes we whispered like conspirators, trading jokes about the librarian's squeaking cart, about our father's handwriting in the ledger, about the cat that slept on the rice sacks. Then Bao turned to the last page, where the debts were listed, and laid my letter beside it. He did not say anything. He straightened the two papers until their edges matched exactly. I listened to the cart squeak past again and found that it no longer seemed funny at all.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From quiet hostility to open reconciliation between the brothers
From conspiratorial humor to a heavy and wordless reckoning
From hopeful planning to excited celebration of the letter
From bored restlessness to irritation at the noisy librarian
items.explanation: 처음에 형제는 공모자처럼 속삭이며 사서의 수레, 아버지의 글씨, 고양이를 두고 농담을 주고받는다. Bao가 빚이 적힌 마지막 장과 합격 편지를 나란히 놓고 말없이 가장자리를 맞추는 순간, 누가 남아야 하는지라는 무거운 현실이 드러난다. 같은 수레 소리가 더는 우습지 않다는 대비가 분위기 변화를 확인해 주므로 B가 정답이다. D는 수레 소리를 표면적으로만 읽은 오독이다.

items.passage: Sell it, Mehrnaz said, and you will be selling the only thing he ever tuned for both of us. Seoyeon did not answer. They stood in the radio repair shop off Oxford Street in Accra, where the technician had just lifted the back from the old valve set their late teacher had left to the two of them jointly. Inside, the tubes glowed amber. Seoyeon had come with a buyer's offer folded in her violin case; her tuition was due in a week. Mehrnaz, who corrected her bowing down to the angle of a wrist, said nothing more. The technician switched the radio on. A highlife station crackled in, then a violin concerto from somewhere far off, faint and slightly flat. Both women leaned toward it at once. Seoyeon heard Mehrnaz hum the correction under her breath, and found herself, without meaning to, humming it too.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A history of the radio is given, followed by an account of its repair.
A disagreement is stated and then settled when one woman agrees to sell.
A dispute is introduced, set aside, and complicated by a shared habit.
A teacher's lesson is presented and then rejected by a defiant student.
items.explanation: 글은 라디오를 팔지 말라는 Mehrnaz의 말로 갈등을 제시하고, Seoyeon의 등록금 사정이 그 갈등을 구체화한다. 이후 두 사람 모두 말을 멈추면서 논쟁은 잠시 보류된다. 라디오에서 음정이 약간 맞지 않는 바이올린 연주가 흘러나오자 두 사람은 똑같이 몸을 기울이고 함께 교정 음을 흥얼거린다. 이 공통된 습관이 판매 결정을 더 어렵게 만들므로 C가 정답이다. B는 결론이 났다고 보았지만 지문에서 결정은 끝내 내려지지 않는다.

items.passage: Port of Spain was still dark when my mother, Pearl, drove me to the diner on the highway for one last breakfast before my flight. I am Cecile, her only child, and I was leaving for a college in Toronto. She slid a wrapped box across the table: a wool scarf in the colors of a school I had not chosen, the one she had hoped for. I thanked her and put it on at once, over a T-shirt, in the heat. She praised how it looked. We ate saltfish and bake and talked about the weather in Canada. Only on the plane did I notice that she had sewn my initials into the fringe, crooked, by hand, the work of several nights. I wore it through every winter that followed, and I never told her that I knew she knew.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A scene of polite pretense is shown and later reframed by a discovery.
A disagreement is recalled and then settled through frank conversation.
A journey is traced in order, ending with the author's arrival at school.
A gift is criticized, and the author then explains why it was returned.
items.explanation: 식당 장면에서 Cecile은 원하지 않은 학교 색의 목도리를 바로 두르고, 어머니는 잘 어울린다고 칭찬하며 둘 다 아무렇지 않은 척한다. 비행기에서 손으로 수놓은 이니셜을 발견한 뒤에야 그 선물에 담긴 어머니의 마음과 서로의 연기가 새롭게 이해된다. 따라서 겉으로 꾸민 장면이 나중의 발견으로 다시 해석되는 구조인 A가 정답이다. B는 솔직한 대화가 없었다는 점, D는 선물을 계속 착용했다는 점과 어긋난다.

items.passage: I had asked Younghee three times to write down the fish stew he made each winter, and three times he had laughed and pointed at the gulls over the ferry terminal, as though the birds kept his accounts. On the morning he meant to sail for his sister's island, I brought a notebook and a pencil to the waiting hall. He took neither. Instead he pressed a paper twist of dried anchovies into my palm, then a knob of ginger, then a pinch of something gray that smelled of smoke. __He named nothing, only closed my fingers over each in turn, the way a man coils rope he expects another to handle.__ When the horn sounded, he walked to the gangway without looking back. I stood a long while in the Busan wind, the notebook still blank under my arm, and found I no longer wished to fill it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Younghee has forgotten the ingredients and is hiding his confusion from the narrator.
It suggests that Younghee resents the narrator's repeated requests and wishes to end the visit.
It indicates that Younghee is handing down the recipe through touch rather than through writing.
It reveals that the narrator has finally persuaded Younghee to record the recipe in lasting form.
items.explanation: Younghee는 레시피를 적어 달라는 요청을 세 번 웃어넘겼고, 공책과 연필도 받지 않은 채 재료를 하나씩 화자의 손에 쥐여 준다. 밑줄 문장은 그가 이름을 말하지 않고 손가락을 감싸 주는 동작을, 다른 사람이 다룰 밧줄을 감는 선원의 습관에 빗대어 전수의 의미를 드러낸다. 마지막에 화자가 공책을 채우고 싶지 않게 된 것도 레시피가 이미 몸으로 전해졌음을 뒷받침하므로 C가 정답이다. A의 망각이나 B의 원망은 지문 근거가 없고, D는 공책이 끝까지 비어 있다는 점과 모순된다.

items.passage: Defne had ruled on harder matters than a broken dryer, but she watched Leopoldina kneel before the machine as if a verdict waited inside it. The girl had come from the courthouse on her lunch hour, still wearing her lanyard, with a screwdriver borrowed from the guard. 'The belt is worn,' Leopoldina said. 'I can tighten it. It will turn again for a month, perhaps two.' Defne said nothing about the rust spreading along the drum's seam, which she had noticed the first week the Istanbul laundromat opened. __She handed over her own coins for the test cycle and sat down to wait, folding her hands in her lap as she once had at the bench.__ The drum shuddered, caught, and began to spin. Leopoldina grinned up at her. Defne nodded slowly, the way she used to nod at lawyers whose arguments were well made and would not, in the end, prevail.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows that Defne doubts Leopoldina's skill and plans to supervise every single step of the repair.
It suggests that Defne regrets leaving the courthouse and misses the authority of her old role.
It reveals that Defne expects the repair to last and wishes to reward the clerk's hard effort.
It conveys that Defne lets the clerk's attempt proceed respectfully despite knowing its limits.
items.explanation: Defne는 드럼 이음매의 녹을 이미 알고 있으면서도 그 사실을 말하지 않는데, 이는 수리가 근본 해결이 아님을 알고 있다는 단서다. 밑줄 문장에서 그녀는 자기 동전을 내주고 판사석에서처럼 손을 모은 채 기다리며, 변론을 끝까지 들어 주는 판사의 태도로 청년의 시도를 존중한다. 마지막의 '잘 짜였지만 결국 이기지 못할 변론'에 대한 끄덕임이 이 해석을 완성하므로 D가 정답이다. A의 감독 의도, B의 향수, C의 영구 수리 기대는 지문의 녹 언급과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Four stones mark the safe path across the dry riverbed below our town in Oaxaca, and Nicolas taught me to count them aloud before I was old enough to ask why. Every crossing, my stepfather named them: the flat one, the split one, the one shaped like a shoe, the last. The summer my scholarship letter came, he walked me to the bus on the far bank. I, Katarzyna, the girl who had never left the valley, talked the whole way about tuition, about the cost of the ticket north, about how he would manage the stall alone. He answered none of it. __At the third stone he stopped, tapped it twice with his boot, and waited until I said its name.__ On the far bank he set down my suitcase and told me the river would be running by the time I came home, and that I should not try to cross it by memory.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Nicolas answering the narrator's worries through a familiar ritual instead of discussion.
It suggests that Nicolas is unsure of the old path and needs the narrator to guide him safely across.
It indicates that Nicolas disapproves of the scholarship and is trying to delay her departure.
It reveals that the narrator has forgotten the stones and must be taught the path once again.
items.explanation: 화자는 등록금과 차비, 가게 운영 걱정을 쏟아내지만 Nicolas는 어느 말에도 대답하지 않는다. 대신 밑줄 문장에서 그는 어릴 때부터 함께 해 온 돌 이름 부르기 의식을 반복하게 하며, 말이 아닌 익숙한 행동으로 화자를 안심시키고 떠나보낸다. 마지막에 돌아올 때는 기억에 의존해 건너지 말라는 당부도 이 의식이 작별의 의미를 지님을 뒷받침하므로 A가 정답이다. B와 D는 길을 모른다는 근거가 없고, C는 그가 직접 버스까지 배웅한 사실과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Flour dusted my stepmother's wrists before the sun was up, and by five she had already shaped forty loaves for an oven she could no longer afford to repair. I was sixteen and had told her, more than once, that the bakery in our Tbilisi lane was finished: the new supermarket sold bread cheaper, and Stanislav, who had fired the oven for my father, was nearly eighty. She never argued. She only set out cups of tea each morning, one for herself and one for Stanislav, and a third, untouched, at my place on the bench. __One morning I sat down and drank it, and she slid the scoring blade across the table toward me without a word.__ I cut the loaves badly. Stanislav laughed until he coughed. Dmitri, my friend from school, asked that afternoon why my hands smelled of yeast, and I told him I was only helping until the place closed. I said that for eleven more years.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows the narrator finally convincing the stepmother that the bakery must be closed.
It marks the narrator's first acceptance of a role the stepmother had quietly kept open.
It suggests the stepmother is testing whether the narrator could replace Stanislav at the oven.
It reveals that the narrator joined the work only to prove the bakery could not survive.
items.explanation: 계모는 화자의 폐업 주장에 반박하지 않고 매일 아침 화자의 자리에 손대지 않은 차 한 잔을 놓아 둔다. 밑줄 문장에서 화자가 그 차를 마시자 계모가 말없이 칼을 건네는데, 이는 계모가 비워 둔 자리를 화자가 처음으로 받아들인 순간이다. 마지막에 '문 닫을 때까지만 돕는다'는 말을 11년 동안 했다는 대목이 그 수락의 지속을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A와 D는 화자가 결국 남았다는 결말과 어긋나고, C는 오븐 담당 교체를 시사하는 근거가 없다.

items.passage: When the band paused between songs, Tommaso came in through the kitchen door of the wedding hall as if he had stepped out for ice twenty minutes earlier instead of nine years. Aaliyah, the bride, did not know him; she saw only that her new mother-in-law set down her fork and did not pick it up again. He wore a pressed suit a size too large and carried a gift wrapped in newspaper. No one asked where he had been, and he offered nothing, only kissed his mother's cheek and took the empty chair by the cake table that someone, it seemed, had been keeping. Gossip along the Delta levees had long since called him a scoundrel. Yet the cake was cut beneath his hand, and the old woman ate two pieces, and the bride, watching, decided that some absences are settled in ways a guest list cannot show.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tommaso?
options: The narrator is openly contemptuous of his failure to explain his long absence.
The narrator is amused chiefly by the awkwardness his arrival causes among the guests.
The narrator is indifferent to his history and attends only to the bride's feelings.
The narrator withholds judgment, implying his return holds meaning gossip overlooks.
items.explanation: 서술자는 Tommaso의 9년 공백을 설명하지 않으며, 그가 늦게 들어온 장면도 비난 없이 담담하게 그린다. 누군가 비워 둔 의자, 어머니가 케이크를 두 조각 먹는 모습 같은 행동 단서는 그의 귀환이 가족에게 의미가 있음을 보여 준다. 소문이 그를 악당이라 불렀다는 언급 뒤에 'Yet'으로 반전시키는 구조가 서술자의 유보적 태도를 드러내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 소문의 시각을 서술자의 시각으로 오독한 것이고, B와 C는 지문의 진지한 관찰과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Who tells a dying man that the salt works he built will be sold by spring? I asked Armand this on my third week, while we raked the evaporation pans outside Beirut and the crust cracked white under our boots. He did not answer. He told me instead to rake slower, so the crystals would not cloud. That evening we carried a tin of the first harvest to Giada's bed, and Armand described the pans to him in detail: how high the brine stood, how the wind had come off the sea. Every word was true. He left out only the letter from the buyers, folded in his breast pocket. Driving back, I said that wasn't lying, exactly. Armand turned the radio up. I have spent years since retelling that drive, and I always slow down at the part where he raked so carefully for a man who would never see the sale.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Armand?
options: Respectful of his care for Giada, though uneasy about what he chose to leave unsaid
Openly critical of what the narrator regards as Armand's deliberate deception of Giada
Dismissive of Armand's silence, which the narrator reads as indifference to his friend
Wholly approving of Armand's decision and certain that it was the only honest choice
items.explanation: 화자는 '모든 말이 사실이었다'고 강조하면서도 Armand가 매각 편지만은 빼놓았다는 점을 굳이 덧붙인다. 돌아오는 길에 '정확히 거짓말은 아니었다'고 말하는 대목에는 판단을 망설이는 불편함이 드러난다. 그러면서도 수년이 지나도록 그가 정성껏 갈퀴질하던 장면에서 늘 이야기를 늦춘다는 마지막 진술은 깊은 존중을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 비판의 강도가 과하고, C는 Armand의 세심한 행동과 모순되며, D는 화자의 머뭇거림을 무시한다.

items.passage:
Hot oil still in my hair, I stand on the platform at Piccadilly
beside Chiara, who has said nothing since the till was counted.
Forty years she ran that kitchen like a ship,
barked at me for every bruised onion, every slack knife.
Tonight she wrapped the knives in a tea towel
and gave them to me, handle first,
the way she taught me, the way you pass something sharp.
Nobody said closing. The sign says Back Soon.
A Manchester tram comes in hissing. She checks her ticket twice.
I want to tell her the onions were never bruised,
that I learned the knife from her wrists, not her shouting.
Instead I hold the towel against my chest
and let her board first, the way she likes.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Chiara?
options: Resentful of the years of harsh criticism Chiara directed at the speaker
Tender and protective, sensing the care beneath Chiara's strictness
Relieved that Chiara's demanding kitchen has finally been shut down
Puzzled by Chiara's silence and wary of provoking her bad temper
items.explanation: 화자는 Chiara가 양파와 칼 때문에 늘 호통쳤다고 회상하지만, 칼을 손잡이부터 건네받는 장면에서 그녀의 가르침을 그대로 따른다. '호통이 아니라 그녀의 손목에서 칼을 배웠다'는 행은 엄격함 뒤의 애정을 화자가 알아보고 있음을 보여 준다. 수건을 가슴에 품고 그녀가 좋아하는 대로 먼저 타게 하는 마지막 행동은 보호하려는 마음을 드러내므로 B가 정답이다. A는 과거 호통만 보고 오독한 것이고, C와 D는 '아무도 폐업이라 말하지 않는' 슬픈 분위기와 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: I was twelve when Mohan came home from the border and took over our grandfather's clock shop in Kochi, and I assumed he did it because no one else would. He was clumsy at first; his hands, which had cleaned rifles for six years, shook over the hairsprings. Still, every evening he cleared a space on the bench and set a loupe in front of me. I complained. Tourists bought quartz watches from the stalls; nobody, I told him, would pay to fix a pendulum. He agreed, and kept handing me the tweezers. I learned to hear the beat of an escapement before I learned to like him again. Now, when customers ask Sunja who taught her, I say my brother, and I let them assume he was a master. He was not. He was a man who practiced late at night so he could stay one lesson ahead of me.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mohan?
options: Resentful, since she believes he pushed an outdated trade onto her unwillingly
Admiring chiefly of the expert skill he showed as a master clockmaker
Affectionate and grateful, valuing his persistence more than his ability
Sympathetic toward him, though convinced that his effort was largely wasted
items.explanation: 화자는 Mohan의 손이 떨릴 만큼 서툴렀다고 솔직하게 말하면서도, 그가 매일 저녁 자리를 마련하고 핀셋을 건넸다는 행동을 반복해 보여 준다. 손님들이 그를 장인으로 여기게 두면서도 '그는 장인이 아니었다'고 덧붙이는 대목은 실력이 아닌 노력에 대한 애정을 드러낸다. 밤마다 한 수업 앞서 연습했다는 묘사가 이를 완성하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 초반의 불평만 본 오독이고, B는 서툴렀다는 진술과 모순되며, D는 화자가 결국 기술을 익혔다는 점과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Callum stepped off my father's boat in the summer of 1912 with a botanist's case and a cough, and asked within the hour why our tea bushes grew only on the western slope above the Galway shore. I was fourteen and found the question rude. Every child on the estate knew the east field was poor ground; my father, Lachlan, said so at supper each night, the way other men said grace. Callum walked the east rows anyway, crumbled the soil between his fingers, and said the trouble was the drainage ditch my grandfather had dug, not the earth. My father thanked him and refilled his cup. The ditch stayed. Callum left on the September ferry, and I rowed him across myself, cross that he had been right and that we would go on as if he had not. I still keep the soil sample he left on our windowsill, labeled in his small hand.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Callum?
options: Scornful of the arrogance he showed in questioning the family's knowledge
Fond of him chiefly because he flattered her father during the visit
Indifferent to his findings, which she regarded as unimportant to the estate
Grudgingly appreciative of the clarity that his outsider's view provided
items.explanation: 화자는 처음에 Callum의 질문을 무례하다고 느꼈지만, 그가 옳았다는 사실에 화가 났다고 고백한다. 그 분노는 Callum보다 아무 일 없다는 듯 살아갈 가족을 향한 것이어서, 그의 지적을 인정하고 있음을 보여 준다. 그가 남긴 흙 표본을 지금도 간직한다는 마지막 행동이 마지못한 존중을 드러내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 첫인상만 본 오독이고, B는 아첨의 근거가 없으며, C는 표본을 간직하는 행동과 모순된다.

items.passage: Taipei's hills were not supposed to hold vineyards, Mingyu told me, which was why he had planted one. We were strangers waiting out a washed-out road on his porch, my rented scooter tipped in the mud, rows of purple grapes dripping behind us. When I said my name was Xinyi, he repeated it twice, as if testing its weight. I asked how he had started. He said a teacher, forty years ago, had read his essay about his father's tea farm aloud and remarked, not unkindly, that it was a good essay about the wrong crop. He laughed telling it. Then he handed me shears and showed me how to cut a bunch without bruising its neighbors. By the time the road crew arrived, my hands were sticky and I had filled two baskets. I never learned what the teacher meant, and I doubt Mingyu had ever settled it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
options: To depict a traveler's frustration at being stranded far from her intended destination
To portray how an offhand comment became a lasting, unresolved motive in a man's life
To explain the farming methods needed to grow grapes in a poorly suited climate
To suggest that Mingyu bitterly resents the teacher who once dismissed his writing
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 요지가 세 곳의 근거를 종합해야 나오고, 오답은 각각 한 곳만 요약한 부분 요지다
items.explanation: Mingyu는 포도밭이 있을 수 없는 언덕이라서 오히려 포도밭을 심었다고 말하며, 그 계기로 40년 전 선생님의 한마디를 웃으며 꺼낸다. 화자가 그 말의 뜻을 끝내 알지 못하고 Mingyu도 풀지 못했을 것이라 짐작하는 대목은 그 말이 여전히 열린 질문임을 보여 준다. 따라서 지나가는 말 한마디가 평생의 일을 이끈 미해결 동기가 되었음을 그리는 것이 목적이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 화자가 오히려 수확을 도운 점과 맞지 않고, C는 세부를 과장했으며, D는 그가 웃으며 이야기한 점과 모순된다.

## 문항
### lit40-hard-01-024 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
I gave you the fishing rod on your twelfth birthday, Errol,
and you leaned it in the corner like a broom.
Consuelo said you wanted books. I heard her
the way the river hears a pebble.
Now we stand on the stone bridge over the Hope,
you with your satchel, I with nothing in my hands,
and neither of us looks down at the water
where I used to fish at your age.
You point to a heron, stiff as a nail.
I almost tell you that my father gave me nothing,
that the rod was my whole vocabulary.
Instead I count the stones in the railing,
each one set by someone who did not explain it.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “the way the river hears a pebble” most nearly suggests
A) that the speaker took in Consuelo's words without changing his course.
B) that the speaker found Consuelo's remark sharp and painful to accept.
C) that Consuelo spoke so softly the speaker could not make out her words.
D) that the speaker and Consuelo often argued by the river about Errol.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
강은 조약돌이 떨어져도 잠깐 물결이 일 뿐 흐름을 바꾸지 않는다. 화자는 아들이 책을 원한다는 Consuelo의 말을 들었지만 여전히 낚싯대를 선물했고, 그것이 자신의 유일한 '어휘'였다고 고백한다. 즉 말을 듣긴 했으나 행동은 바뀌지 않았다는 뜻이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 충격을, C는 소리 크기를 비유의 뜻으로 오해한 것이고, D는 근거가 없다.
### lit40-hard-01-025 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Piper had captained the girls' team at our school in Vigo for three seasons, and by the night of the winter dinner she ran the gymnasium like a deck: tables in rows, chairs squared, her grandmother's empanadas at the head. Lucia had arrived from Buenos Aires in October and came along that evening without being on any list; I think she slipped in behind the volunteers carrying folding chairs. She brought a tray of alfajores and set it down, hesitating, at the far corner. I watched Piper notice it. She said nothing. She lifted her grandmother's platter and slid it down the table until the two trays touched, then pulled up a chair at that end, the wrong end by her own rules, and sat. For the rest of the night the table listed toward Lucia's corner, a boat trimmed to an unexpected weight, and no one tried to set it straight.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a boat trimmed to an unexpected weight” most nearly suggests
A) that the table was overloaded with food and close to collapsing.
B) that the gathering had rebalanced itself around the newcomer.
C) that Piper had lost control of the dinner she carefully planned.
D) that the guests were uneasy and wished Lucia had stayed home.

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
Piper는 체육관을 배의 갑판처럼 엄격히 정돈했지만, Lucia의 쟁반을 보고 말없이 할머니의 접시를 옮겨 붙이고 자신의 규칙상 '잘못된' 끝자리에 앉는다. 배가 새 무게에 맞춰 균형을 잡는다는 비유는 모임 전체가 새로 온 사람을 중심으로 다시 자리 잡았다는 뜻이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 비유를 물리적으로 읽은 오독이다. C와 D는 기운 테이블을 실패나 불편으로 본 표면 해석으로, 아무도 바로잡지 않았다는 서술과 맞지 않는다.
### lit40-hard-01-026 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Three rules governed the galley of the training ship docked at Manila that summer: knives point down, nothing left on the burners, and no one cries where the cook can see. I was nineteen, newly hired to teach English to the cadets, and Anh, the cook, let me hold class at his steel tables between meals. Shira, the quietest cadet, would not answer me for weeks. So I made a plan. I asked her to translate Anh's recipes for the others, and she did, fluently, in front of everyone. The cadets applauded. Anh grinned. Shira folded the recipe card into smaller and smaller squares until it was the size of a stamp. That night I scrubbed the same pot three times. The plan had worked, I kept telling myself; the success sat in me like a meal eaten standing up.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “like a meal eaten standing up” most nearly suggests
A) that the narrator was too busy teaching to sit down and eat properly.
B) that the narrator felt physically ill from rough conditions aboard ship.
C) that the narrator's achievement felt hasty and gave no real satisfaction.
D) that the narrator was eager to celebrate the success with the whole crew.

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
계획은 성공해 박수가 나왔지만, Shira는 레시피 카드를 우표 크기까지 접으며 불편함을 드러낸다. 화자가 같은 냄비를 세 번 닦고 '성공했다'고 스스로를 설득하는 모습도 마음이 편치 않음을 보여 준다. 서서 급히 먹은 식사의 비유는 성공이 허겁지겁 지나가 아무런 포만감을 주지 않았다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A와 B는 비유를 글자 그대로 읽었고, D는 화자의 불편한 심정과 반대된다.
### lit40-hard-01-032 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 tone_shift
[지문]
Two cups of espresso cooled on the zinc counter of the station cafe in Bologna while Fiorella untied the ribbon around their mother's letters. Anneke's train to Rotterdam left at 4:10, and her suitcase held everything she meant to keep. They read the first letters aloud, laughing at the spelling, at the recipes copied into the margins, at a long complaint about a neighbor's goat. Fiorella did the voices. Then Anneke unfolded one dated the spring she had first gone away, years ago, and read it silently. Fiorella waited for the voice, and none came. Anneke set the page face down, squared it against the others, and picked up her ticket, turning it over as though it might list a different time. Fiorella retied the ribbon slowly, making the bow twice.

[질문] Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
A) From bitter resentment of the mother to forgiving acceptance of her flaws
B) From playful shared reminiscence to a hushed tension about the departure
C) From anxious haste about the train to relief that there is time to spare
D) From detached curiosity about the letters to open grief expressed in tears

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
전반부에서 두 사람은 편지를 소리 내어 읽으며 철자와 염소 이야기에 웃고, Fiorella는 목소리 연기까지 한다. Anneke가 처음 떠났던 봄의 편지를 말없이 읽는 순간부터 웃음은 사라지고, 기차표를 뒤집어 보거나 리본을 천천히 두 번 묶는 동작으로 긴장이 드러난다. 따라서 장난스러운 회상에서 이별을 앞둔 조용한 긴장으로 바뀌는 B가 정답이다. D는 눈물을 흘린다고 했지만 지문의 감정은 끝까지 겉으로 드러나지 않는다.
### lit40-hard-01-033 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 tone_shift
[지문]
Clay forgives nothing. Tamika's husband had said that to every student who walked into the studio on Seventy-First Street, and for thirty years the neighborhood had repeated it as proof of his genius. She was boxing his glazes when Ngozi arrived with the kiln parts, a lanky boy who lingered to admire the famous blue bowls on the top shelf. My uncle fired those, he said cheerfully. Your husband paid him in lunch. Tamika laughed, assuming a joke, and handed him a bowl to carry. Ngozi turned it over and showed her the mark scratched faintly into the foot, two initials that were not her husband's. She set the box of glazes down. For a while she simply moved along the shelf, bowl by bowl, turning each one over with care.

[질문] Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
A) From grief-stricken mourning to cheerful celebration of the husband's work
B) From suspicious hostility toward Ngozi to grateful trust in his account
C) From affectionate pride in a legacy to a sober, searching reconsideration
D) From casual indifference about the bowls to an outraged public accusation

C) Relieved that Chiara's demanding kitchen has finally been shut down
D) Puzzled by Chiara's silence and wary of provoking her bad temper

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
화자는 Chiara가 양파와 칼 때문에 늘 호통쳤다고 회상하지만, 칼을 손잡이부터 건네받는 장면에서 그녀의 가르침을 그대로 따른다. '호통이 아니라 그녀의 손목에서 칼을 배웠다'는 행은 엄격함 뒤의 애정을 화자가 알아보고 있음을 보여 준다. 수건을 가슴에 품고 그녀가 좋아하는 대로 먼저 타게 하는 마지막 행동은 보호하려는 마음을 드러내므로 B가 정답이다. A는 과거 호통만 보고 오독한 것이고, C와 D는 '아무도 폐업이라 말하지 않는' 슬픈 분위기와 맞지 않는다.
### lit40-hard-01-048 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude
[지문]
I was twelve when Mohan came home from the border and took over our grandfather's clock shop in Kochi, and I assumed he did it because no one else would. He was clumsy at first; his hands, which had cleaned rifles for six years, shook over the hairsprings. Still, every evening he cleared a space on the bench and set a loupe in front of me. I complained. Tourists bought quartz watches from the stalls; nobody, I told him, would pay to fix a pendulum. He agreed, and kept handing me the tweezers. I learned to hear the beat of an escapement before I learned to like him again. Now, when customers ask Sunja who taught her, I say my brother, and I let them assume he was a master. He was not. He was a man who practiced late at night so he could stay one lesson ahead of me.

[질문] Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mohan?
A) Resentful, since she believes he pushed an outdated trade onto her unwillingly
B) Admiring chiefly of the expert skill he showed as a master clockmaker
C) Affectionate and grateful, valuing his persistence more than his ability
D) Sympathetic toward him, though convinced that his effort was largely wasted

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
화자는 Mohan의 손이 떨릴 만큼 서툴렀다고 솔직하게 말하면서도, 그가 매일 저녁 자리를 마련하고 핀셋을 건넸다는 행동을 반복해 보여 준다. 손님들이 그를 장인으로 여기게 두면서도 '그는 장인이 아니었다'고 덧붙이는 대목은 실력이 아닌 노력에 대한 애정을 드러낸다. 밤마다 한 수업 앞서 연습했다는 묘사가 이를 완성하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 초반의 불평만 본 오독이고, B는 서툴렀다는 진술과 모순되며, D는 화자가 결국 기술을 익혔다는 점과 맞지 않는다.
### lit40-hard-01-049 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude
[지문]
Callum stepped off my father's boat in the summer of 1912 with a botanist's case and a cough, and asked within the hour why our tea bushes grew only on the western slope above the Galway shore. I was fourteen and found the question rude. Every child on the estate knew the east field was poor ground; my father, Lachlan, said so at supper each night, the way other men said grace. Callum walked the east rows anyway, crumbled the soil between his fingers, and said the trouble was the drainage ditch my grandfather had dug, not the earth. My father thanked him and refilled his cup. The ditch stayed. Callum left on the September ferry, and I rowed him across myself, cross that he had been right and that we would go on as if he had not. I still keep the soil sample he left on our windowsill, labeled in his small hand.

[질문] Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Callum?
A) Scornful of the arrogance he showed in questioning the family's knowledge
B) Fond of him chiefly because he flattered her father during the visit
C) Indifferent to his findings, which she regarded as unimportant to the estate
D) Grudgingly appreciative of the clarity that his outsider's view provided

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
화자는 처음에 Callum의 질문을 무례하다고 느꼈지만, 그가 옳았다는 사실에 화가 났다고 고백한다. 그 분노는 Callum보다 아무 일 없다는 듯 살아갈 가족을 향한 것이어서, 그의 지적을 인정하고 있음을 보여 준다. 그가 남긴 흙 표본을 지금도 간직한다는 마지막 행동이 마지못한 존중을 드러내므로 D가 정답이다. A는 첫인상만 본 오독이고, B는 아첨의 근거가 없으며, C는 표본을 간직하는 행동과 모순된다.
### lit40-hard-01-051 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 main_idea_or_purpose
[지문]
Taipei's hills were not supposed to hold vineyards, Mingyu told me, which was why he had planted one. We were strangers waiting out a washed-out road on his porch, my rented scooter tipped in the mud, rows of purple grapes dripping behind us. When I said my name was Xinyi, he repeated it twice, as if testing its weight. I asked how he had started. He said a teacher, forty years ago, had read his essay about his father's tea farm aloud and remarked, not unkindly, that it was a good essay about the wrong crop. He laughed telling it. Then he handed me shears and showed me how to cut a bunch without bruising its neighbors. By the time the road crew arrived, my hands were sticky and I had filled two baskets. I never learned what the teacher meant, and I doubt Mingyu had ever settled it.

[질문] Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
A) To depict a traveler's frustration at being stranded far from her intended destination
B) To portray how an offhand comment became a lasting, unresolved motive in a man's life
C) To explain the farming methods needed to grow grapes in a poorly suited climate
D) To suggest that Mingyu bitterly resents the teacher who once dismissed his writing

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
Mingyu는 포도밭이 있을 수 없는 언덕이라서 오히려 포도밭을 심었다고 말하며, 그 계기로 40년 전 선생님의 한마디를 웃으며 꺼낸다. 화자가 그 말의 뜻을 끝내 알지 못하고 Mingyu도 풀지 못했을 것이라 짐작하는 대목은 그 말이 여전히 열린 질문임을 보여 준다. 따라서 지나가는 말 한마디가 평생의 일을 이끈 미해결 동기가 되었음을 그리는 것이 목적이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 화자가 오히려 수확을 도운 점과 맞지 않고, C는 세부를 과장했으며, D는 그가 웃으며 이야기한 점과 모순된다.
